As a lifelong fan of the Man of Steel who grew up on all those comics you mentioned, and the animated series, I largely agree with you OP. The Man of Steel remains a top2 comic book movie for me.

Having said that I completely understand where other lifelong fans of the character are coming from in their dislike (even hate) of the film. It's not because the movie doesn't borrow elements from some of those critical comics, it clearly does, but it's the execution of those ideas in the film which leaves much to be desired.

There's also an element of trying to do **too much** in the movie, and then not following through with ideas/emotional development. Killing the villain can work, but it's execution was jarring (violent to watch) and was followed up by a lighthearted scene immediately after, which made it even more jarring. I also am someone that's always believed the colors are too muted.

These seemingly "nitpicky," things are actually critical in how an audience will perceive a film.

So while I personally love the film, I also clearly see all the faults with it and how others of goodwill can absolutely detest it. There are many critics that aren't fans of the character, and their only reference point is the earlier version, and that certainly lead to an unfair (imho) score. But there are plenty of fans of the character out there that think the film didn't do the character justice either.

I think we are in agreement. Let me just expand on my initial comment. What I'm saying is that a statement like "i pulled myself up by my bootstraps" or the more common variation of **"they** *just need to pull themselves up by their bootstraps"* is almost always said in a jerkish way because the mindset behind those that say it/live by it is jerkish. This isn't about whether or not someone has overcome great hardship and worked hard in life; it's about the mindset they have once they overcome it.

* Do they recognize that despite all the hard work *they* put in, that there was still someone, something, or *some* circumstance that benefited them at *some* point? (i.e. that company that hired them in the first place was deciding to take a chance on them. Or did someone lend/give them $10 for gas so they could get to their interview? Or was there a free addiction services entity that helped them get clean? Did someone decide to put in the time to mentor them? etc...) Edit: And do they **then give credit where credit is due** for these things, or do they sweep this help under the rug and claim to have needed no help to achieve what they achieved?
* Do they recognize that despite all their hardship there is literally *always* someone in the world that has had it even worse in their life?
* Once they overcome their circumstances do they recognize that paying-it-forward is important, whether through deed, words, or charity?
* Do they support policies that will help others overcome their circumstances like they did?

So when I hear the phrase "pull up by bootstraps" or some variation of that I'm instantly skeptical of that person because it's rarely said in a non-jerkish way in my experience.
